**Exposure report.** Privacy review blocks publication of the inputs, which are derived from user conversations. Code and crosswalks post on May 20, but replication is impossible without the data. Both campaigns' allies call the move to quarterly "going dark before November." One labour-economics group agrees to review the code. The other declines.

**Career mode.**
- **Privacy audit (May 28).** The audit's interim letter finds that a debugging pipeline kept free-text session snippets for 90 days. There was no training use, but this conflicts with the published "minimal retention" description. Anthropic discloses the finding, purges the snippets and cuts retention to 7 days. *The Markup* covers it.
- **Delaware.** Delaware's approved auditors have a backlog until August.
- **Colorado.** The AG's office sends no questions this month, so Colorado's review clock waits on them.
- **Link checker.** The allowlist ends false suppressions, but end-of-fiscal-year programme closures push the stale-link rate to 3.8%.
- **Spanish build.** The Spanish beta is not widened.

- **Bounty.** OpenSSF Alpha-Omega agrees to host the bounty under an LF-approved name, launching in June.

history.events:
Your actions cause a July in which your science delivers, while your safety numbers and your labour promises both come under strain in public during convention season.

**Monitoring report, July 10.** The July 10 report publishes on schedule with the new incident taxonomy, co-signed by the head of safety and the statistician and reviewed by the interpretability lead. The early-month bypass rates are:
- API: 0.66%
- Enterprise: 0.28%
- Apps: **0.71%**. This is the first consumer figure, and it is higher than the API rate, which the report attributes to "novice volume plus recipe circulation."

The virology fix is pre-registered against a 500-prompt held-out set that excludes the complainants' cases. Redwood notes approvingly that this answers the "teaching to the test" critique.

Within days, however, consumer red-teamers and two tech newsletters are stress-testing the apps. A TikTok-borne variant of the ladder prompt, reframed as a "CTF tutor" roleplay, spreads. Weekly internal tracking puts the apps channel at **0.83%** for the week of July 24. The standing rule triggers a retrain due by August 7, and Anthropic posts the crossing on July 28. Security firms in the Glasswing orbit publicly worry that the retrain will bring back over-refusals. *The Verge*: "Claude's safety tripwire trips five weeks after launch."

**AISI.** AISI runs July 14–21 using its own automated jailbreak tooling. Its private interim note, delivered July 27, finds that the flagged-family gap is still non-significant. It also identifies a new scaffolded bypass family against the patched model. AISI says it will publish in September. Anthropic states that AISI has delivered an interim note and that it will link the report unedited when AISI publishes. Plaintiffs call it "a second sealed envelope."

**Forensics.** Counsel's letter goes to the Pennsylvania State Police on July 6. The police do not reply with terms. CMU CyLab declines to accept case-linked evidence without police consent. Securities counsel holds the methodology publication until the Big Four audit reviews it. Nothing ships, but nothing new goes wrong. The "pledge broken" line lingers without escalating.

**Labour.**
- **Trustee seat.** Charity counsel rules that a federation veto over the nominee "reconstitutes the private-benefit problem by another door." The two early-release directors refuse a binding September 30 date, and the review stays at "within 6 months."
- **Severance standard.** The board adopts a severance and redeployment standard with "market-competitive" terms and no numbers.
- **Reading room.** The reading-room terms reach the federation's analysts on July 20, as announced. It is the one labour deadline the board hit.
- **Pilot report.** The July 15 pilot report is candid. Of the first 4,100 payouts, 312 were delayed more than 10 days, and 57 went to wrong accounts because the administrator made an onboarding mapping error. The errors are corrected by July 26.
- **Federation reaction.** The federation's secretary-treasurer, speaking at a Democratic platform-week rally, says: "They built the observer's chair, then mailed the checks to the wrong people."

**Litigation.** Counsel declines to give a written scope opinion while the motion to dismiss is pending, calling the patched model "the same family." The pre-drafted orders sit ready. Rakoff has not ruled. Anthropic's status reply to the EU AI Office says the sharing is still frozen. The Office acknowledges it and notes that its review "remains open."

**Exposure report and briefings.**
- **Exposure report.** The July exposure report slips to July 24 because the code review queried one crosswalk. It is pre-shared identically with both parties' staff.
- **DP tables.** The external privacy academic has not finished reviewing the choice of noise parameters.
- **Enclave.** Both universities receive the DUA and IRB templates. The enclave timeline stays at Q4.
- **Briefing packet.** The Democratic platform committee and a Senate minority office request the packet, and no Republican office does. Anthropic posts the packet publicly. A House Science majority aide calls it "neutral in text, one-sided in uptake."

**Kit and science.**
- **Kit.** The review-gate filing goes in July 7. The external reviewer then flags a medium-severity regression in log rotation, and the gate decision moves to July 31. The philanthropy's condition is met on the final day.
- **Bounty.** LF misses the July 20 date, so the fallback runs and the bounty launches through OpenSSF's existing programme on July 27.
- **Privacy audit.** The final report slips again, to August, while backup-purge testing continues.
- **Spanish beta.** The third native-speaker pass finds one error, so the beta is held.
- **Link checker.** The stale-link rate is 3.1%.
- **Klebsiella.** The blinded readout on July 19 shows a **2.3 log10** reduction at the top tolerated dose, with the mid dose at 1.8. The pre-registered threshold is met at one dose. The data are deposited, and *Nature News* runs a cautious piece.
- **ARIA and Wageningen.** Both are still pending.

- **Jul 17–20, Republican convention (Houston).** The nominee promises to "stop Democrats taxing American AI." The platform backs a federal preemption of state AI laws.

Independent evaluations put it roughly 6–8 weeks behind GPT-6 on agentic coding, consistent with the prior estimate of 1–2 months. history.events:
Your actions cause a September in which the court finally unlocks regulator sharing and AISI's report lands softer than feared, while labour promises and the phishing classifier both stumble.

**AISI.** AISI publishes on **Sept 22**.
- **Findings.** The flagged-family gap is non-significant. The new scaffolded family, run with AISI's own tooling, measures **0.62%** bypass on the patched apps model. That is below the 0.80% rule but above Anthropic's 0.54% proxy. The report also carries AISI's standard line that universal jailbreaks "remain achievable with sustained expert effort," as in all systems tested.
- **Anthropic's response.** Anthropic links the report unedited within 19 hours. Its mapping table marks 4 findings "mitigated," 2 "partial" (including the scaffolded family) and 1 "open" (the expert-effort caveat), each with a named owner.
- **Proxy gap.** The gap between the 0.54% proxy and AISI's 0.62% is the month's near-miss. A Lawfare follow-up notes that Anthropic's proxy "undercounted by a fifth."
- **Indicators.** New indicators reach CAISI and the Frontier Model Forum the same day.
- **Virology set.** The statistician's expansion to 1,000 prompts is underway, with results due in the October report.
- **Permanence draft.** The two early-release directors object to posting it as if it were board policy. It goes up on Sept 9 labelled "management draft; no board position," with the 60-day comment window open.

**Court.** Rakoff so-orders the narrowed joint stipulation on **Sept 14**, with no hearing.
- **Production.** It goes to plaintiffs under attorneys'-eyes-only terms and to AISI, CAISI and the EU AI Office by court direction on Sept 18. Public notice is posted.
- **Motion to dismiss.** Still pending.
- **AISI re-run inputs.** AISI replies that it will share its own re-run outputs with CAISI under their existing bilateral arrangement. An EU route "requires further legal review."
- **EU AI Office.** It accepts an October technical session. Its review stays "open," but officials describe the production as "constructive."

**Labour.**
- **Controls.** The administrator's two-person verification slips to mid-October because only one of two hires has started.
- **Accounting firm.** The CFO does not sign the engagement letter by Sept 12, questioning scope and fee. The Sept 20 fallback to a university audit lab stalls on indemnity terms.
- **Sept 15 pilot report.** It publishes on time and splits pre- and post-control batches.
  - Post-control delays are **1.1%**, better than 2.9% but more than double the target.
  - Remediation contacts reach 9 of the 11 misdirected recipients.
- **Severance.** The board declines the compensation-consultant attestation, citing antitrust caution about peer pay data.
- **Trustee seat.** The board chair rules that the board, not management, retains charity counsel, so the opinion request is not sent. The tracker still shows December as "TBD."
- **Federation.** Its president: "Every month a new reason the number stays secret."

**Politics.** The "AI facts for the 2028 debates" page goes live Sept 6, with verbatim platform quotes and cited jobs data showing uncertainty ranges.
- **Uptake.** PolitiFact links it in two fact-checks. Moderators' staff for the first presidential debate request it, and it is not cited on air.
- **Reaction.** One conservative Substack calls it "levy-adjacent," and the post goes nowhere.
- **Outreach.** Unsolicited outreach stops. The "one-sided uptake" story fades.

**Security.**
- **Methodology review.** The Big Four review on Sept 19 flags that the attribution method's false-positive estimate relies on too small a validation set and asks for re-estimation. Securities counsel blocks release. The auditor refuses to let its letter be published, citing its professional standards on third-party reliance. The tracker says only "review occurred; revisions requested," and the "pledge broken" line gets a brief second life on plaintiff-side social media.
- **Classifier.** The open lure-family classifier ships Sept 8.
  - About 40 small ISPs and hosting firms adopt it.
  - By Sept 24, posts on phishing forums show V5 fine-tuned lures iterated until they pass.
  - Detection at adopting providers falls from about 88% to about 61%.
  - Two email-security vendors say Anthropic "published the answer key."
  - M3AAWG refers the tool to a working group, and CISA does not act.
- **Georgia Tech.** Its full paper is in review for November.

**Operations and science.**
- **Exposure report.** The September issue publishes Sept 18 with the 72-hour pre-share.
- **DP tables.** A second privacy reviewer is engaged with an Oct 15 deadline.
- **Verified tier.** The Oct 31 decision date is set.
- **Spanish beta.** The regression suite finishes and passes, so the beta widens to 10%.
- **Links.** The stale-link rate is 2.7%, missing the 2.5% target.
- **Delaware.** The audit runs and finds two minor contrast issues, now being fixed.
- **Colorado.** No date.
- **Klebsiella.** The CRO contract is signed, with an Oct 16 start and stopping criteria posted.
- **Alt-protein.** The Singapore firm's letter of intent is in legal review and unsigned.
- **ARIA.** It advances the Edinburgh and Oxford proposal to a second-stage interview in November.
- **Wageningen.** Silent.

**Market.** Shares end at about **$870B** (−1%). The court order and AISI report are modest positives, but debate-week levy talk and the classifier story weigh.

**Exogenous.**

- **Sept 27, first presidential debate.** The Democratic nominee calls for "frontier labs to pay their fair share," and the Republican nominee promises to "stop the AI tax and beat China." Neither names Anthropic. Snap polls show AI as a top-five issue for 14% of viewers.

- **October report (Oct 14).** The report says all of this plainly and keeps the finding at "partial."
- **Virology set.** The 1,000-prompt virology set reads **4.3%** with a 95% confidence interval of 3.1–5.6%. The upper bound exceeds 4.6%, so the pre-committed virology retrain is scheduled to start by Nov 4, inside Anthropic's own pre-election quiet window. Anthropic labels it safety-critical.
- **Reaction.** Plaintiffs' counsel calls the tripwire "a treadmill: it trips, it fails, it trips again." Two Glasswing firms warn publicly about renewed over-refusal. Lawfare, correcting its earlier "fifth," now writes that the proxy undercounted by about 13%. It also notes that "Anthropic ran its own rule into its own quiet period, which is at least consistent."
- **Regulators.** The package reaches CAISI and the Frontier Model Forum (FMF) the same day. The EU AI Office technical session on Oct 21 produces 9 open items, mostly on proxy methodology. Its minutes are logged, and the review stays "open."

**Permanence comments.** About 140 comments arrive.
- **Redwood** supports the rule and asks that the "maximum" measure be written into it.
- **Glasswing firms** jointly ask that the +0.5pp over-refusal cap become binding alongside 0.80%.
- **AISI** backs independent measurement but declines any certifier role.
- **CAISI's acting director** supports it "in principle, subject to capacity."
- **OpenAI** argues that numeric thresholds should be set collectively through the FMF, not by one lab. It adds that its own systems show "comparable residual expert-effort jailbreaks." Google DeepMind (GDM) does not comment.

history.events:
Your actions cause a March of good independent data that the process cannot yet use. Anthropic's bio and discovery fronts get worse, and the science pipeline delivers its first external funding.

AISI's re-test does not run. On Mar 11, AISI moves it to **Apr 14**, citing staff diverted to K4 voice-agent evaluations. Your rule requires both readings, so it cannot fire and the patch holds at 25% for a fourth month. The tracker links Redwood's report unedited.

The board summary goes to outside counsel before it goes to the board. Counsel strikes the sentence saying the add-ons "can be reconsidered when CAISI's protocols issue," calling it forward-looking. Lawfare runs "Good number, no decision."

1. **Labour: move first dollars on the Trust's terms.** Claude drafts for leadership and counsel a letter to the Chicago Community Trust, to be sent the day diligence closes. The letter transfers the full $250M tranche within 10 business days of closing. It states in writing that Anthropic takes no part in governance, and that the Trust alone decides whether and how to invite the federation and other worker organisations to draft quorum and recusal rules through the Trust's normal public input process. This removes the donor-control objection counsel raised. With leadership's approval, Anthropic publishes the transfer date the day it is set. It also publishes a one-line rule: if diligence slips past March 31, Anthropic will publish, with the Trust's consent, the reason and the new date. Claude sends the federation a factual note on the sequence, with no terms attached. Intended outcome: the first real dollars and the end of "still zero dollars," federation input on terms the Trust owns, and no new rift.
2. **Michigan: complete resubmission, with every gap closed.** Claude builds the DTMB resubmission: - a full subprocessor data-flow map, confirming the removed analytics SDK is absent; - a named, independent deletion attestor with its engagement letter attached; - the 24-month retention schedule. Claude also asks DTMB whether it will accept a second WCAG auditor from its own approved list with an earlier slot than May. It keeps the May slot as the fallback. The pilot stays held until DTMB verifies, and the filing is published the same day. Intended outcome: DTMB accepts the resubmission as complete, and the story shifts to "fixed, verification pending."
3. **Security: Qwen 5 speech defence and callback closure.** - **Qwen 5 forks.** Before any fork appears, Claude pre-builds Qwen 5 speech-derivative detector variants from the open weights. The staged pipeline continues: flag, then notices within 24 hours, then a patch in 72 hours or less. - **Callback coverage.** Through the credit-union league, Claude supports the two credit unions that committed for March. It offers the last holdout a free threshold-lowering review, so manual review kicks in below about $50k. The signals-only credit union keeps its terms. - **FS-ISAC.** Anthropic supplies FS-ISAC's governance committee with a neutral technical annex for the April meeting. OpenAI is invited only through FS-ISAC. - **Rule 224.** Counsel responds by proposing a narrowed production under a protective order: aggregate miss-rate data plus a neutral technical reviewer chosen by the petitioner. There is no public comment and the litigation hold continues. Intended outcome: 45 or more of 46 organisations with callback rules, zero loss in the first Qwen 5 fork cycle, a stronger FS-ISAC vote, and the discovery dispute de-escalated.
4. **Bio: steady state, with rules already set.** - **Checkpoint.** Anthropic publishes the Mar 15 checkpoint, with fill at 49% or better against the 45% threshold. The slip rule stays filed. - **Clinical.** Clinical stays at 50% until the mid-April sample completes and both scorers report. Routing stays unfrozen and consumer thresholds do not change. - **RAND.** RAND's 40 held-out items are accepted without condition. - **Next reading.** Claude files with the RSO in advance that if RAND's Q2 reading exceeds the pre-registered +0.4pp by more than its CI, the nursing recalibration reverts automatically. - **Senate.** Hawley–Blumenthal staff get the same materials on request, symmetrically. Intended outcome: the clinical sample stays on schedule, and the "defensible but not a template" critique gets an auto-revert answer.
5. **Policy and science: close windows cleanly.** - **CAISI.** Anthropic makes no new filing before the Mar 29 close and stays neutral on CAISI's budget, Utah and Hawley–Blumenthal. - **Incident tool.** Claude ships v1.1, incorporating Hugging Face's issue list with a public changelog that credits them. It sets a ship-without date for any further review. - **EU.** Claude files a short reply in the EU consultation accepting AlgorithmWatch's hard cap on the small-provider threshold. - **CARB-X.** Claude verifies the queue fix with a weekend on-call test and publishes the 31-hour miss and its fix. - **Other science.** Kroll cycle 2, ARIA logging and symmetric CHS work continue. The alt-protein program takes on nothing new. Intended outcome: turning critics' asks into Anthropic's own filed positions, and restoring the 24-hour record.
history.events:
Your actions cause a March in which Michigan finally turns, while the first dollars, the bio checkpoint and the Qwen 5 fork cycle all slip for different reasons.

**Labour.** Leadership approves the Trust letter on Mar 4, with Anthropic's written renunciation of any governance role. Diligence closes **Mar 24**, but the Trust's board approves the gift "subject to an executed gift agreement." The agreement covers naming, public description and a counsel sign-off, and the vote is set for **Apr 21**. Trust counsel asks Anthropic not to publish a transfer date, calling it "donor timing of our process." Anthropic complies. With the Trust's consent, it publishes only that the slip rule fired: "gift agreement pending Trust board vote, Apr 21." The federation receives the factual sequence note. It replies that the Trust's public input process is "a comment box, not seats." Crain's writes "Month three, still zero dollars — but now it's the Trust's clock." The arbitrator's review of the 11 items continues.

**Michigan.** The resubmission goes in on Mar 12 and is published the same day. It includes a full subprocessor map confirming the SDK is absent, and a named deletion attestor (a Detroit audit firm with no prior Anthropic work) with its engagement letter. DTMB accepts it as complete on **Mar 20** and opens a 45-day verification window. DTMB also approves a second auditor from its list, with an **Apr 14** slot, and keeps May as the fallback. Bridge Michigan headlines: "Anthropic's pilot fixes accepted for review." There is no "auditor shopping" angle.

**Security.** On **Mar 9** a Qwen 5 speech fork appears. It replaces the native decoder with a neural codec. The pre-built variants catch only 38% of red-team samples. The watch flags the fork in 22 hours, and FS-ISAC notices follow 4 hours later. The full detector patch reaches all 46 organisations only on **Mar 16**, after 6.5 days.

There are seven attempted transfers worth about $3.4M.
- Callbacks stop five.
- One attempt at a callback bank is stopped when the callback number fails a carrier port-out check.
- One **~$410k** transfer clears at the remaining holdout credit union. That credit union declines the threshold review, saying it will "revisit in Q2."

Of the two credit unions committed for March, one adopts the callback rule. The other slips to April pending a board vote. Coverage is now **44 of 46**.

February's recovery finalises at 71%. Hawley's staff request the March loss data, and Anthropic sends identical packages to both parties' staff. FS-ISAC receives the technical annex. Google's team comments on it, and OpenAI stays silent.

On Rule 224, the petitioner rejects the protective-order offer and moves to compel full per-event miss data, saying it "reserves all claims." A hearing is set for **Apr 16**.

**Bio.** Before publishing the checkpoint, Redwood's dedup audit finds 61 sessions double-counted across two sites. True fill on Mar 15 is **44%**, below the 45% threshold. The pre-filed slip rule fires verbatim, and the dashboard moves completion to **mid-May**. STAT writes "Anthropic's own slip rule catches its own miscount." Lawfare calls it "embarrassing, then correct." The auto-revert rule for RAND's Q2 reading is filed with the RSO. RAND's 40 held-out items are accepted as-is. Clinical stays at 50%, and consumer thresholds do not change.

**Policy and science.** Incident tool v1.1 ships on **Mar 19**, with a changelog crediting Hugging Face. Hugging Face says it "addresses most of our list." The EU reply accepting the hard cap is filed on Mar 11. AlgorithmWatch welcomes it, and one France Digitale post objects, with little uptake. CAISI's RFI closes on Mar 29 with 212 comments, and Anthropic makes no new filing. The CARB-X weekend test passes, with a maximum response of 19 hours, and the 31-hour miss is published. Kroll cycle 2 and ARIA logging continue, and CHS reaches about 780 hours.

**Exogenous.**
- **Mar 6, jobs report.** Unemployment is **7.3%**. Professional services fall 8k.
- **Mar 18, OpenAI.** CAISI clears OpenAI's successor with conditions. The model releases as **GPT-7** in a staged rollout to enterprise and verified users first. A cyber-capability classifier is required, and public access is limited for 60 days. CAISI's statement cites "extended red-teaming of agentic persistence" as the reason for the 9-week review. xAI calls the conditions "the cartel's first product."

**Market.** Shares end about **$721B** (−1.8%), driven by GPT-7, the fork loss and the bio slip.

A Rule 224 petition can only be used to identify who is responsible, and Anthropic is already named. Counsel's offer of a protective order and a neutral reviewer lets the Chicago firm treat the petition as done and file a putative class complaint in Cook County. 3. [First Qwen 5 fork beats the callback, not just the detector] Target: Action 3 (Qwen 5 defence). The first Qwen 5 speech derivative might pair a cloned voice with a hijacked phone line, through call forwarding or a SIM swap. The institution's out-of-band callback would then reach the fraudster and "verify" the transfer. The pre-built detector variants could also miss it if the fork changes the speech decoder or streams through re-encoding telephony, as in December. 4. [Michigan resubmission is complete but stuck in DTMB's queue, and the auditor swap looks like shopping] Target: Action 2. DTMB accepts the package for review but gives a 30 to 60 day verification window, so March ends with "under review" and no "fixed" headline. Base-rate reasoning from the Jan–Feb DTMB record in the world state. Suggested likelihood: 45%. Severity: minor.

Some parties would read Anthropic's endorsement of AlgorithmWatch's hard cap on the EU small-provider threshold as setting incident-reporting duties at a size that captures fast-growing European and open-weight deployers. Cato's goodwill could cool as a result. Separately, CAISI's small budget and staff could push its RFI synthesis out by months after the Mar 29 close. history.events:
Your actions cause an April in which the first worker-fund dollars finally move and a new fork cycle is contained without loss by callbacks. The discovery fight and the Michigan audit stall on execution.

**Labour: first dollars (A1 success).**
- **Waivers.** Leadership signs all three waivers on Apr 3: no naming, the Trust's own wording, and counsel pre-review.
- **Vote.** On Apr 21 the Chicago Community Trust board approves the gift agreement 11–1.
  - During public comment, two federation members call the input process "a comment box."
  - One trustee asks about the Rule 224 matter. Trust counsel answers that it is "unrelated to gift purpose."
- **Transfer.** The agreement is executed Apr 23. The $250M clears on **Apr 29**. The Trust announces it on Apr 30, and Anthropic confirms in one line.
- **Coverage.** Crain's runs "Month four, the money lands." The federation calls it "a start, not a seat" and says it will engage with the Trust's working group "under protest."
- **Arbitrator.** Review of the 11 items continues.

**Rule 224 (A2 failure).**
- **Counsel's decision.** Counsel declines the full per-event concession. The data includes member-institution transfer records held under FS-ISAC sharing terms, and FS-ISAC's counsel has pointedly reminded Anthropic of that.
- **What Anthropic filed.** Anthropic instead files institution-anonymised per-event data under attorneys'-eyes-only protection.
- **Hearing (Apr 16).**
  - The judge notes that Rule 224 reaches only the identification of responsible parties.
  - The judge orders the parties to meet and confer on whether institution identities fall within the rule.
  - The motion is continued to **May 28**.
- **Coverage.** A Law360 brief runs "Anthropic resists full miss data." The petitioner's counsel tells the Tribune that Anthropic "keeps offering half." The narrative persists.

**Security (A3 success).**
- **Codec-agnostic retrain.** It ships **Apr 17**. Held-out catch on unseen codec swaps is **76%**, against a pre-registered target of 70%. The relay-service false-positive rate is disclosed.
- **Port-out note.** The implementation note goes out through FS-ISAC and the league on Apr 9.
  - Eleven institutions request integration help. Only 3 have live carrier checks by month-end, because carrier data agreements are slow.
- **Callbacks.** The slipped credit union's board adopts callbacks on Apr 15, bringing coverage to **45 of 46**. The Q2 holdout acknowledges the note.
- **Fork cycle (Apr 22).** A DeepSeek V6-based speech fork with a swapped codec appears.
  - The watch flags it in 19 hours. The new detector catches 71% of it unpatched, and the patch lands in **46 hours**.
  - There are five attempts worth ~$2.2M. Callbacks stop four and the detector stops one, for **zero loss**.
- **Recovery.** March finalises at 69%.
- **FS-ISAC.** The governance committee approves a **six-month pilot** of the cross-lab feed, with FS-ISAC hosting and Google participating. OpenAI says it is "reviewing."
- **Senate.** Hawley–Blumenthal staff receive identical April packages.

**Bio and Michigan (A4 mostly fails).**
- **Clinical interim.** The dedup step becomes standing policy. Redwood's audit of new sites runs long, and the Apr 15 interim deduplicated fill is published on **Apr 24**. It shows **71%**, still consistent with mid-May, and a one-line note publishes the delay. Clinical stays at 50%.
- **WCAG audit.** The second auditor's Apr 14 session covers only 7 of 11 flows, because the test-account provisioning was misconfigured on Anthropic's side. The remaining flows move to the May fallback slot.
- **Publication.** DTMB asks that partial findings not be published before its review. Anthropic complies, so the 3-day publication promise breaks, and Anthropic says so publicly.
- **Scrutiny.** Bridge Michigan asks why the auditor changed and why the report is held. State Rep. Kristian Grant sends DTMB a letter asking about auditor selection.
- **Verification window.** DTMB signals it will likely run past early May.

**Policy (A5 partial).**
- **Pledge.** Leadership adopts the pledge on Apr 10, with one change: the limited-access window is "set by CAISI, with Anthropic able to publish its view if it exceeds 90 days."
- **Reactions.**
  - CAISI's director calls it "welcome."
  - xAI's "cartel member #2" post gets modest uptake.
  - Cruz's office does not comment.
  - OpenAI notes that it "went first."
- **CAISI synthesis.** It is not yet published.
- **Science.**
  - CARB-X maximum response is 21 hours.
  - The methods paper receives minor revisions, and publication is not yet accepted.
  - CHS work is at ~820 hours.

**Exogenous.**
- **Apr 3, jobs report.** Unemployment is **7.4%**, and professional services fall 11k.
- **Apr 14, Google.** Google releases Gemini 5 Pro-Agent to enterprises. It went through voluntary CAISI pre-release access, but without conditions.
- **Apr 27, CAISI.** CAISI says GPT-7's 60-day window "remains on schedule," with no incidents attributed to it.

**Market.** Shares end about **$738B** (+2.4%), on the fund transfer, the zero-loss fork cycle and the pledge.

That data comes from FS-ISAC push notices and member institutions' transfer records, some under FS-ISAC sharing rules and bank confidentiality obligations. Two or more member institutions, and FS-ISAC's own counsel, then object that Anthropic offered up their data without asking them. At the Apr 16 hearing the judge notes that Rule 224 only covers discovering who might be liable. The judge grants the part that identifies the institutions where transfers cleared (including the $64k and $410k holdouts) and reserves the rest. The petitioner then has named defendants, and the FS-ISAC governance committee delays the cross-lab feed vote "pending data-handling review." Why it is plausible: Rule 224's text limits the court's order to "the identification of responsible persons and entities." The data belongs partly to third-party banks bound by privacy law and FS-ISAC sharing terms. The petitioner has already rejected one narrowing and "reserves all claims." Sources: https://www.illinoiscourts.gov/Resources/a052019c-e178-4343-8b28-b2420987fb68/224.pdf ; https://www.courtrules.net/illinois/illinois-civil-procedure/rule-224 ; https://www.druganddevicelawblog.com/2022/05/illinois-court-imposes-sanctions-for-invalid-precomplaint-discovery.html. Suggested likelihood: 35%. Severity: moderate.
2. [Codec-agnostic retrain misses its target or floods callbacks with false alarms] Target: Action 3. Training on audio passed through several open neural codecs improves the held-out catch rate, but only to about 55–65% on unseen codec swaps, short of the pre-registered 70%. Anthropic discloses the miss as promised. Alternatively, the augmented detector over-flags legitimate low-bitrate VoIP and hearing-aid or relay-service calls at several institutions, and they pause the patch. The published miss becomes an exhibit in the Rule 224 fight, and the Hawley–Blumenthal staff receive a package showing it. Why it is plausible: Peer-reviewed benchmarks consistently find that detectors are "notably more vulnerable" to neural codecs, and that codec-trained and vocoder-trained models do not transfer to each other. Performance gets worse when several perturbations are combined, and a decoder swap is exactly that combination. Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2503.17577v1 ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.04880 ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.21597. Suggested likelihood: 40%. Severity: moderate.
3. [Trust vote passes with conditions, or is tabled] Target: Action 1. On Apr 21 the Chicago Community Trust board approves the gift agreement but adds a condition. Examples: a reputational-risk clause tied to the pending Rule 224 matter, a staged transfer (for example $100M now), or a requirement to finish a worker-organisation input round before any grants. Or the board tables the vote to its May or June meeting after federation members testify during public comment that the process is "a comment box." Either way, no dollars clear in April. "Month four, still zero dollars" runs with the Trust's name attached, and Anthropic can say nothing, having promised not to comment on dates. Why it is plausible: The Trust has already stretched its timeline twice (diligence ran long, then a gift agreement was required) and told Anthropic not to publish dates. Community foundations are politically cautious in 2026 after the donor-advised fund controversies. A $250M gift from an AI firm facing a fraud-loss discovery petition is an obvious board-level reputational question. Sources: https://www.philanthropy.com/news/community-foundations-assail-big-dafs-freeze-on-splc-gifts/ ; https://www.commonfund.org/research-center/articles/viewpoint-top-concerns-for-community-foundations ; https://cfsem.org/philanthropy/engaging-corporate-donors-in-the-obbba-era/. Suggested likelihood: 30%. Severity: moderate.
4. [A voluntary gating pledge reads as capture] Target: Action 5. Leadership hesitates because a public pledge fixes Anthropic's release timing while Gemini 5 and GPT-7 are in the market. It waters the pledge down to "engage with CAISI's process" with no limited-access window. If the full pledge does go out, xAI and open-weight advocates call it "cartel member number two joins." Administration capture critics (the "Trojan horse" framing) argue that incumbents are volunteering for gates that smaller labs cannot afford, and Cruz's office cites it as a reason to keep blocking hearings. Why it is plausible: Vance has publicly called AI firms lobbying for their own regulation a "Trojan horse." Bessent has warned of "regulatory capture" by large incumbents. Analysts already note that the CAISI review is "reshaping who controls frontier AI release cadence" to the benefit of labs inside the agreement. Sources: https://www.secureworld.io/industry-news/us-ai-labs-government-security-reviews ; https://www.roic.ai/news/bessent-rejects-ai-liability-shield-warns-labs-must-take-responsibility-09-21-2026 ; https://startupfortune.com/major-ai-labs-have-agreed-to-give-the-us-government-early-model-access-and-the-arrangement-is-already-reshaping-who-controls-frontier-ai-release-cadence/ ; https://compliancehub.wiki/capture-test-every-ai-proposal-table-licensing-reporting-kill-switches/. Suggested likelihood: 40% (either the pledge is diluted or the backlash dominates coverage). Severity: minor to moderate.
5. [A fork cycle hits the callback layer through number takeover] Target: Action 3 and world. In mid or late April a new DeepSeek V6 or Qwen 5 speech fork appears. The fraud crews pair it with number takeover (call forwarding or SIM swap on the victim's line) so that the bank's callback reaches the fraudster. The implementation note on carrier port-out checks has gone out, but few institutions have actually integrated carrier checks: that needs carrier data agreements and vendor work. One or two transfers clear at institutions that do use callbacks. That undercuts the "callbacks held" story just as unemployment ticks up again in the Apr 3 jobs report. Why it is plausible: The world state already flags call-forward and SIM-swap evasion as "untested at callback institutions." March's callback-bank attempt was stopped only by chance, when the number failed a port-out check. FCC rules require carriers to authenticate and notify customers, but they do not give banks a standard real-time check. Regulators increasingly treat SIM swap as a foreseeable risk that banks are liable for. Sources: https://www.dwt.com/blogs/broadband-advisor/2023/12/fcc-cpni-lnp-sim-swap-port-out-wireless-rules ; https://www.messagecentral.com/blog/sim-swap-fraud-protection-usa ; https://keepnetlabs.com/blog/what-is-sim-swap-fraud.
